newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. to set up a new Angola mission when troops go.
newsitem.headline: U.N. to set up a new Angola mission when troops go.

text.p: With tensions rising in Angola, the United Nations said on Friday it would slow the withdrawal of its existing 4,000 troops and set up a new mission of 86 military observers and 345 civilian police.
The new operation, to be known as the U.N. Observer Mission in Angola or by its Portuguese acronym MONUA, officially takes over on July 1.
But the U.N. troops are to withdraw slowly with two reduced infantry battalions remaining until sometime in September. Another infantry company would stay to guard U.N. property until November.

Secretary-General Kofi Annan, in a report to the Security Council, recommended 86 military observers, 345 civilian police, about 50 human rights monitors, and assorted other civilian personnel in the new mission.

Currently, the United Nations has close to 5,000 troops, military observers and civilian police from more than 30 countries in Angola. It is helping to implement the agreement signed in Lusaka, Zambia, in November 1994 that ended nearly two decades of civil war in the former Portuguese colony.

In the last few days, the Angolan army has pushed deeper into diamond-rich areas held by UNITA former rebels in the northeast and at least 65 soldiers were wounded in clashes on Thursday, according to news reports from Angola.

The war in neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo, formerly Zaire, saw the participation of both Angolan government troops and UNITA, despite their respective denials, on opposite sides of the conflict.

The Luanda government said its operation in the north was intended to flush out armed refugees who had come across the border from the new Congo but analysts said this was a pretext to retake diamond-rich territory under the control of UNITA.

"The overall military situation in the country has remained calm although recent developments in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have contributed to a worrisome rise in tension in the northern provinces of Angola," the report said.
Annan's report said the peace process was on track but U.N. troops were still needed to guide the demobilization of UNITA soldiers, which has been moving slowly.

He said 71,055 UNITA soldiers had registered at U.N. demobilization centres as of June 1, with more than 35 per cent of them deserters, But only 10,700 former UNITA rebels have joined the national army out of an expected 26,300.

Missing from the report, however, is how many UNITA troops had never disarmed despite the peace agreements. U.N. and diplomatic sources said some UNITA soldiers were returning from neighbouring Congo while others were in the country.
Consequently, they said the government considered a criminal anyone they found with a gun.

The report also said that despite persistent difficulties, the formation of a power-sharing government was "moving in a positive direction." UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi, however, has still not appeared in the capital of Luanda and diplomatic sources said he wanted a bodyguard of 2,000 rather than the 200 agreed earlier.

The report also said the government's hold on administrating the vast areas under UNITA control was proceeding at a slow pace and the "psychological and political barriers between the parties are still wide."
